title: Hepatocellular Carcinogenesis: Signaling, Stromal Heterogeneity and Immune Escape
content: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) develops through cooperation between altered hepatocytes, chronic liver injury and a stromal and immune environment. Genomic alterations and signaling abnormalities provide a rationale for treatment development, but pathway activation rarely identifies therapeutic dependence alone. This narrative review connects hepatic stellate-cell states, tumor-cell plasticity, genomic instability and four major signaling pathways with antigen presentation, immune exclusion and clinical treatment evidence. Targeted searches were updated through 6 October 2026, retaining foundational work and prioritizing recent studies. Single-cell and spatial analyses reveal that stellate cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts can exert opposing effects according to their state and location. Similarly, CTNNB1-associated signaling can favor immune exclusion, but mutation status does not fully capture immune context or establish universal resistance to checkpoint combinations. Intratumoral dendritic-cell and lymphocyte organization, suppressive myeloid niches and humoral responses provide complementary explanations of treatment heterogeneity. Randomized trials support selected antiangiogenic and checkpoint combinations in unresectable HCC, while negative trials and updated adjuvant results demonstrate the limits of extrapolating biological rationale across regimens and disease stages. The synthesis distinguishes experimental causality, patient-level association and clinically validated benefit. Translation requires compartment-specific target assessment, representative sampling and prospective biomarker evaluation within a defined treatment setting, alongside assessment of liver reserve.
